title: Limon Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Limon wells are typically 30 feet deep, with finished well costs modeled at $7,000-$13,600.
h1: What Limon, Colorado Wells Are Really Like
intro_html:
For a rural property near Limon, the local well records point to relatively shallow wells and generally usable production. Among permitted wells within the Limon area, the median reported depth is 30 feet, and the middle half falls between 20 and 50 feet. Reported yields are also stronger than many buyers expect, with a 10.0 gallons-per-minute median.

That picture comes from permit records, not a guarantee for a particular lot. Only 315 wells are recorded as constructed, 418 report a total depth, 65 report a pump yield, and 12 report a static water level. Use the nearby records to frame a drilling bid, then verify the proposed well location, septic layout, water quality and permitting before closing.

sections.heading: Limon’s shallow wells reflect plains geology
sections.html:
Limon sits in a plains setting where the drilling model is based on alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. The local depth median is 30 feet, with the middle half of reported wells between 20 and 50 feet. The 90th percentile is 61 feet, and 98% of the depth records are under 100 feet.

That is useful when reviewing a driller’s proposal. A bid that assumes a very deep hole deserves questions, although depth can change quickly from one parcel to the next. The deepest recorded well is 350 feet, so shallow conditions are common rather than guaranteed. Nearby records from Genoa, Hugo and Matheson can provide additional context, but the wells closest to the proposed house and septic field matter most.

sections.heading: What a Limon well may produce
sections.html:
The reported yield median is 10.0 gallons per minute, with the middle half between 10.0 and 15.0 gallons per minute. The records show 58% producing between 5 and 15 gallons per minute, while 29% report more than 15 gallons per minute.

Low-yield wells are still part of the local picture: 6% report under 1 gallon per minute and another 6% report between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Only 65 wells report a pump yield, so these percentages describe the available records rather than every permitted well. Ask for a yield test, storage-tank sizing and the intended household use. An exempt household-use well is generally subject to Colorado’s 35 gallons-per-minute pumping limit, but that limit does not promise that the aquifer will produce that rate.

sections.heading: The Limon water table: shallow, but not a proven trend
sections.html:
Only 12 permitted wells in the Limon records report a static water level. Those measurements have a median depth to water of 20 feet, with the middle half between 17 and 27 feet. For excavation and well construction, that suggests groundwater may be encountered fairly close to the surface in some locations.

The available facts do not provide a water-level series by decade, so they do not establish that the water table is dropping or rising. A static level is also not the same as a pumping level. Ask the driller for nearby well logs, the expected pumping drawdown and the recovery behavior after testing. A shallow water table can reduce drilling depth while increasing the importance of proper casing, grout and surface drainage.

sections.heading: Permit history shows continued drilling around Limon
sections.html:
Limon’s permit record stretches from the 1950s through the newest permit year, 2025. The busiest decade in the supplied history was the 2000s, with 146 permits, followed by the 2010s with 94 and the 1990s with 86. The 2020s account for 27 permits so far in the record.

The use mix is not limited to homes: 28% are domestic or household wells, 23% stock, 5% irrigation and 39% monitoring. The most frequent driller names are Authorized (Pe, Pg), with 147 records; Eastwood Drilling (Eastwood, Francis), with 68; and Eastwood Drilling LLC (Eastwood, Robert D.), with 20. Treat permit history as evidence of local experience, not an endorsement. Confirm current licensing, insurance and the exact scope of work before hiring.

sections.heading: Estimated well drilling cost near Limon
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a drilling rate of $35 to $55 per foot for Limon’s alluvium and plains sedimentary rock. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole itself models to about $1,000 to $1,600. That is only the hole, not a functioning water system.

The modeled finished-well range is about $7,000 to $13,600, including the pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical work. A written bid should identify casing and grout, pump equipment, testing, electrical service, trench length and any difficult access. Compare bids using the same scope. A shallow hole can still become an expensive project if the lot needs a long utility trench, special access or additional site work.

sections.heading: Limon risks to check before you buy
sections.html:
Water quality deserves specific attention. The mapping shows 30 PFAS sampling or contamination sites within about 10 miles of Limon. It shows 0 historic mine features and 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Those facts do not determine the quality of a particular well, but they are a reason to test the existing well or budget for a full baseline test before relying on it.

Low yield and dry holes remain possible even in an area with a 10.0-gallon-per-minute yield median. Review nearby logs for depth, aquifer name, construction and production. Most permits name an unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifer, with 467 wells; 58 name Alluvial and 55 name Quaternary Alluvium. Before building, confirm well and septic separation, soil suitability, driveway access, electrical routing and any augmentation-plan requirements for the intended use.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Limon, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Limon is 30 feet. The middle half of wells falls between 20 and 50 feet, and the 90th percentile is 61 feet. Most are shallow: 98% of reported depths are under 100 feet. Still, the deepest record is 350 feet, so a nearby shallow well does not guarantee the same result on your parcel.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Limon?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $35-$55 per foot. At the 30-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $1,000-$1,600. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $7,000-$13,600. Ask contractors to separate drilling from equipment, testing, trenching and electrical so bids can be compared accurately.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Limon?
faq.a: The reported yield median is 10.0 gallons per minute, and the middle half is 10.0-15.0 gallons per minute. Records show 6% under 1 gallon per minute and 6% between 1 and 5 gallons per minute. Only 65 wells report a yield, so require a yield test and discuss storage needs before buying or building.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Limon?
faq.a: Do not assume an untested well is safe to drink. There are 30 PFAS sampling or contamination sites mapped within about 10 miles, although the records show 0 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites. Test the specific well for common contaminants and PFAS, review its construction, and retest after a new well is completed or property conditions change.

faq.q: Are there many wells around Limon, Colorado?
faq.a: The Colorado DWR records contain 603 permitted wells within the Limon area, with 315 recorded as constructed. Permit activity runs from the 1950s through 2025. The records include domestic, stock, irrigation and monitoring wells, so not every nearby permit represents a household water source. Check the closest constructed wells and their logs before relying on area averages.
